```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7,
                      fig.height = 4.5)
```

```{r setup}
library(imisr)
```

Calibration estimates the inputs of a simulation model that cannot be
observed directly by making the model's outputs agree with data, called
*calibration targets*. Bayesian calibration combines (1) prior distributions
for the inputs, (2) a likelihood that compares model outputs with the
targets, and (3) the model, which maps inputs to outputs (Menzies et al.,
2017). IMIS then samples the posterior distribution of the inputs, and
running the model on those samples propagates the calibrated uncertainty to
any outcome.

This vignette calibrates two cohort state-transition models included in the
package: the Sick-Sicker model and a three-state cancer relative survival
model (see `?example_models`).

## The Sick-Sicker model

A cohort of 25-year-olds moves each year between four states: healthy (H),
sick (S1), sicker (S2) and dead (D). We calibrate three inputs:

* `p_S1S2`: annual probability of progressing from S1 to S2;
* `hr_S1`, `hr_S2`: hazard ratios of death in S1 and S2 relative to H.

The targets, in `sick_sicker_targets`, are observed survival and disease
prevalence over 30 years and the proportion of the sick who are in S1 at
years 10, 20 and 30, each with a standard error.

```{r targets, fig.height = 3.5}
lst_targets <- sick_sicker_targets
v_target_names <- names(lst_targets)
str(lst_targets$PropSick)

old_par <- par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
for (s_target in v_target_names) {
  df_target <- lst_targets[[s_target]]
  plot(df_target$time, df_target$value,
       ylim = range(0, df_target$lb, df_target$ub), pch = 20,
       xlab = "Year", ylab = "Proportion", main = s_target)
  arrows(df_target$time, df_target$lb, df_target$time, df_target$ub,
         angle = 90, code = 3, length = 0.02)
}
par(old_par)
```

### Prior

Independent uniform priors over plausible ranges. Both functions loop over
the parameters, indexing the bounds by name, and handle all draws of a
parameter at once:

```{r prior}
v_param_names <- c("p_S1S2", "hr_S1", "hr_S2")
v_lb <- c(p_S1S2 = 0.01, hr_S1 = 1, hr_S2 = 1)  # lower bounds
v_ub <- c(p_S1S2 = 0.50, hr_S1 = 12, hr_S2 = 25) # upper bounds

sample_prior <- function(n_samp) {
  m_param_samp <- matrix(NA_real_, nrow = n_samp,
                         ncol = length(v_param_names),
                         dimnames = list(NULL, v_param_names))
  for (s_par in v_param_names) {
    m_param_samp[, s_par] <- runif(n_samp, min = v_lb[[s_par]],
                                   max = v_ub[[s_par]])
  }
  m_param_samp
}

calc_log_prior <- function(v_params) {
  if (is.null(dim(v_params))) v_params <- t(v_params) # vector to 1-row matrix
  v_lprior <- rep(0, nrow(v_params))
  for (s_par in v_param_names) {
    v_lprior <- v_lprior + dunif(v_params[, s_par], min = v_lb[[s_par]],
                                 max = v_ub[[s_par]], log = TRUE)
  }
  v_lprior
}
```

`calc_log_prior()` must be a normalized density (here
`dunif(..., log = TRUE)`) for the marginal likelihood to be correct. Where it
is `-Inf`, IMIS does not run the model at all.

### Likelihood

Each target is treated as normally distributed around the model output, with
its reported standard error. Each target has its own line, so a target that
needs a different distribution (binomial, Poisson, ...) can get one.

`imis()` passes a matrix with one parameter set per row. Simulation models run
one parameter set at a time, so `calc_log_lik()` runs the model on each row.
Some parameter sets inside the prior ranges are impossible: when `p_S1S2` is
large and `hr_S1` is high, the probability of staying in S1 becomes negative
and `sick_sicker_markov()` stops with an error. `tryCatch()` gives those
parameter sets a log-likelihood of `-Inf` (a likelihood of zero).

```{r likelihood}
calc_log_lik <- function(v_params) {
  if (is.null(dim(v_params))) v_params <- t(v_params) # vector to 1-row matrix
  n_samp <- nrow(v_params)
  m_llik <- matrix(-Inf, nrow = n_samp, ncol = length(v_target_names),
                   dimnames = list(NULL, v_target_names))
  for (j in seq_len(n_samp)) {
    l_out <- tryCatch(sick_sicker_markov(v_params[j, ]),
                      error = function(e) NULL)
    if (is.null(l_out)) next # impossible parameter set: log-likelihood -Inf
    # TARGET 1: survival
    m_llik[j, "Surv"] <- sum(dnorm(lst_targets$Surv$value,
                                   mean = l_out$Surv,
                                   sd = lst_targets$Surv$se, log = TRUE))
    # TARGET 2: prevalence
    m_llik[j, "Prev"] <- sum(dnorm(lst_targets$Prev$value,
                                   mean = l_out$Prev,
                                   sd = lst_targets$Prev$se, log = TRUE))
    # TARGET 3: proportion of the sick in S1
    m_llik[j, "PropSick"] <- sum(dnorm(lst_targets$PropSick$value,
                                       mean = l_out$PropSick,
                                       sd = lst_targets$PropSick$se,
                                       log = TRUE))
  }
  rowSums(m_llik)
}

calc_log_lik(c(p_S1S2 = 0.105, hr_S1 = 3, hr_S2 = 10))
calc_log_lik(sample_prior(5))
```

Alternatively, write the log-likelihood for a single named parameter vector
and let `imis()` do the loop with `vectorized = FALSE`; `catch_errors = TRUE`
then turns model errors into `-Inf` and reports how many there were.

### Calibrate

```{r calibrate}
set.seed(2026)
fit <- imis(calc_log_lik, calc_log_prior, sample_prior, verbose = FALSE)
fit
```

```{r diagnostics}
plot(fit)
```

The posterior is far more concentrated than the prior:

```{r marginals, fig.height = 3.5}
plot(fit, type = "marginals")
```

```{r pairs, fig.height = 6}
plot(fit, type = "pairs")
```

### Do the calibrated outputs match the targets?

Run the model on the posterior resample and compare the 95% posterior
predictive bands with the targets:

```{r predictive, fig.height = 3.5}
m_post <- as.matrix(fit)
l_sims <- lapply(seq_len(nrow(m_post)),
                 function(i) sick_sicker_markov(m_post[i, ]))

old_par <- par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
for (s_target in v_target_names) {
  df_target <- lst_targets[[s_target]]
  m_out <- do.call(rbind, lapply(l_sims, `[[`, s_target))
  m_band <- apply(m_out, 2, quantile, probs = c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975))
  plot(df_target$time, df_target$value,
       ylim = range(0, df_target$lb, df_target$ub, m_band), pch = 20,
       xlab = "Year", ylab = "Proportion", main = s_target)
  polygon(c(df_target$time, rev(df_target$time)),
          c(m_band[1, ], rev(m_band[3, ])),
          col = adjustcolor("steelblue", 0.3), border = NA)
  lines(df_target$time, m_band[2, ], col = "steelblue", lwd = 2)
  arrows(df_target$time, df_target$lb, df_target$time, df_target$ub,
         angle = 90, code = 3, length = 0.02)
}
par(old_par)
```

The posterior resample can now replace the prior in a probabilistic
sensitivity analysis, so that cost-effectiveness results reflect what the
calibration targets say about the inputs.

## Non-identifiability: the cancer relative survival model

In the three-state cancer relative survival (CRS) model, patients without
evidence of disease develop metastases with annual probability `p_Mets`, and
patients with metastases die with probability `p_DieMets`. Survival depends
on the two probabilities symmetrically, so survival data cannot tell which is
which (Alarid-Escudero et al., 2018):

```{r crs-symmetry}
all.equal(crs_markov(c(p_Mets = 0.12, p_DieMets = 0.05)),
          crs_markov(c(p_Mets = 0.05, p_DieMets = 0.12)))
```

The posterior therefore has two modes, mirror images across the diagonal.

`sample_prior()` and `calc_log_prior()` read the parameter names and bounds
by name, so they work unchanged once these are redefined. Only the
likelihood, which runs the model and compares it with the targets, is new:

```{r crs-setup}
lst_targets <- crs_targets
v_target_names <- names(lst_targets)
v_param_names <- c("p_Mets", "p_DieMets")
v_lb <- c(p_Mets = 0.04, p_DieMets = 0.04) # lower bounds
v_ub <- c(p_Mets = 0.16, p_DieMets = 0.16) # upper bounds

calc_log_lik <- function(v_params) {
  if (is.null(dim(v_params))) v_params <- t(v_params) # vector to 1-row matrix
  n_samp <- nrow(v_params)
  m_llik <- matrix(-Inf, nrow = n_samp, ncol = length(v_target_names),
                   dimnames = list(NULL, v_target_names))
  for (j in seq_len(n_samp)) {
    l_out <- tryCatch(crs_markov(v_params[j, ]), error = function(e) NULL)
    if (is.null(l_out)) next # impossible parameter set: log-likelihood -Inf
    # TARGET 1: survival
    m_llik[j, "Surv"] <- sum(dnorm(lst_targets$Surv$value,
                                   mean = l_out$Surv,
                                   sd = lst_targets$Surv$se, log = TRUE))
  }
  rowSums(m_llik)
}
```

The optimization stage (`n_optim`) looks for local modes before the
importance sampling begins:

```{r crs}
set.seed(2018)
fit_crs <- imis(calc_log_lik, calc_log_prior, sample_prior, n_optim = 5,
                verbose = FALSE)
fit_crs
```

```{r crs-pairs, fig.height = 5}
plot(fit_crs$resample, col = adjustcolor("black", 0.2), pch = 20,
     xlim = c(v_lb[["p_Mets"]], v_ub[["p_Mets"]]),
     ylim = c(v_lb[["p_DieMets"]], v_ub[["p_DieMets"]]))
abline(0, 1, lty = 2)
points(fit_crs$centers, col = "red", pch = 8)
```

Each mode holds about half of the posterior:

```{r crs-split}
mean(fit_crs$resample[, "p_Mets"] > fit_crs$resample[, "p_DieMets"])
```

Here the posterior mean falls in the valley between the modes, where the
model fits the targets poorly, and the marginal summaries and the
correlation between the two parameters describe neither mode. Report the
modes, or add
targets that separate the two parameters (for example, the proportion of
survivors with metastases), instead of summarizing a multimodal posterior by
its mean.

## Slow models: running in parallel

Both models here run in a fraction of a millisecond, so parallel evaluation
would only add overhead. For a microsimulation or a model that takes
seconds per run, evaluate the likelihood on several workers:

```{r parallel, eval = FALSE}
library(future)
plan(multisession, workers = availableCores(omit = 1))
fit <- imis(calc_log_lik, calc_log_prior, sample_prior, parallel = TRUE)
plan(sequential)
```

Each batch of draws is split into one block of rows per worker, and each
worker calls `calc_log_lik()` once on its block, so the cost of sending work
to the workers is paid once per block rather than once per model run.

613-624.
